prompt.context: It's late 2006, and our client is a PE firm looking to acquire a company in the emerging smartphone industry. There are currently only two firms in the market: SmartCo and PhoneCo. Our client has decided to definitely purchase one of the firms, but they've hired us to help them figure out which one.
prompt.question: How would you approach this problem? Which of the two companies — SmartCo or PhoneCo — should our client acquire?

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider the possibility of Apple entering the market?
clarifying_info.a: The iPhone was announced in January 2007 and launched in June 2007, so it shouldn't be a factor in the initial decision.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other competitors we should be aware of?
clarifying_info.a: In the real world there were more than two firms, but this is a simplified case — what you know about RIM, Motorola, Nokia, etc. doesn't necessarily apply.

clarifying_info.q: What is the investment horizon / exit timeline?
clarifying_info.a: Our client cares about the value of the firm at an exit in 5 years, so a DCF won't be necessary.

clarifying_info.q: What are the unit economics for each company?
clarifying_info.a: Variable costs are $150 per unit for SmartCo and $200 per unit for PhoneCo. Price is $250 per unit for SmartCo and $300 per unit for PhoneCo. Ignore fixed costs.

exhibits.title: Mobile Phone Market (2007 est.)
exhibits.shows: Pie-style breakdown of the mobile phone market into three segments — Business, Prosumer, and Consumer — each showing total market size and current smartphone penetration as a percentage of that segment.

exhibits.title: Customer Survey — All Segments (scale 1–5)
exhibits.shows: Two survey questions answered across all customer segments: (1) importance of each smartphone attribute and (2) ratings of SmartCo and PhoneCo on each attribute.

exhibits.title: Customer Survey by Segment (scale 1–5)
exhibits.shows: The same two survey questions broken out into Business segment customers and Consumer segment customers separately, showing attribute importance and company ratings for each group.

framework: Valuation Economics: Revenues (price × quantity) and Costs (fixed and variable) for each firm — who has better unit economics and margin?
Market Size & Growth: Size and growth trajectory of each customer segment (Business, Prosumer, Consumer) for smartphones over the 5-year horizon
Customer Segmentation: Which segments exist, how large are they, and which company appeals to which segment?
Product & Competitive Positioning: How do SmartCo and PhoneCo rate on attributes customers care about by segment?
Technology & IP: Patents or other technological advantages that create defensible moats
Barriers to Entry: How easily can each company's offering be replicated by a new entrant?
Exit Value Driver: Which company will command a higher valuation at exit in 5 years given segment growth dynamics?

questions.prompt: Question 1 (Market Size Math): Our client expects the mobile phone market as a whole to grow 5% over the next 5 years. Our client also expects smartphones' share of the mobile market to grow 50% for businesses, 100% for prosumers, and 200% for consumers over the next 5 years. What will the smartphone market be in Year 5 for each segment? What does that mean for us?
questions.guidance: Candidate should grow total market by 5%, then apply the new smartphone penetration rates to calculate Year 5 smartphone market size per segment. Approximation is explicitly fine — exact numbers would take too long. The key insight is that while all three segments end up roughly equal in absolute size (~$40-47b), the consumer segment still has massive headroom (only 15% penetration vs. 75% for business), making it the most attractive growth opportunity. The acquisition target should be whichever firm appeals to consumers.

math.setup: Step 1: Grow total market by 5%. Step 2: Apply new smartphone share (current share × growth multiplier) to Year 5 total market.
steps: Business: Total market Y5 = $60b × 1.05 = $63b. New smartphone share = 50% × (1 + 50%) = 75%. Smartphone market Y5 = $63b × 75% = $47.25b (was $30b, growth = $17.25b)
Prosumer: Total market Y5 = $80b × 1.05 = $84b. New smartphone share = 25% × (1 + 100%) = 50%. Smartphone market Y5 = $84b × 50% = $42b (approx $40b, growth = ~$20b)
Consumer: Total market Y5 = $300b × 1.05 = $315b. New smartphone share = 5% × (1 + 200%) = 15%. Smartphone market Y5 = $315b × 15% = $47.25b (approx $45b, growth = ~$30b)
math.answer: Year 5 smartphone markets: Business ~$47b, Prosumer ~$40b, Consumer ~$45b. All segments are roughly equal in Year 5, but the consumer segment has the most room for future growth (only 15% penetration vs. 75% for business). Prioritize the company that appeals to consumers.

questions.prompt: Question 2 (Customer Survey — Aggregate): Here's some data from a survey of all smartphone customers. What does this mean for our client? Is there any other information you'd want to know?
questions.guidance: This is a red herring. A bad response over-interprets the aggregate numbers. A good response notes the two phones are more or less equal to all customers combined. A great response recognizes the data is an aggregate across segments that may behave very differently, and proactively asks for a segment-level breakdown before drawing conclusions.

questions.prompt: Question 3 (Customer Survey — By Segment): Here's that same survey broken out into two segments. What does this mean for our client?
questions.guidance: A good response identifies that SmartCo appeals to consumers (rates 4.9/4.8/4.4 on Style/Price/Apps, the attributes consumers value most) while PhoneCo appeals to businesses (rates 4.7/4.5/4.0 on E-mail/Web/Screen, the attributes business customers value most). If asked, prosumers are a mix but lean slightly toward SmartCo. A great response immediately ties this to the market size finding from Question 1 and recommends acquiring SmartCo unprompted: consumers are the largest growth segment and SmartCo is clearly the consumer-preferred phone.

questions.prompt: Bonus Question (if time permits, after candidate correctly recommends SmartCo): Based on your recommendation, our client has decided to purchase SmartCo. But before they sign the deal, Apple announces they're releasing the iPhone. Does your recommendation change?
questions.guidance: There is no single correct answer; the candidate is evaluated on structured reasoning. Three defensible positions: (1) SmartCo is still the best bet — the consumer market is large enough for multiple players, SmartCo scores 4.7/5 on style and 4.8/5 on price so Apple may not easily displace it, and the iPhone could equally threaten PhoneCo in business/prosumer segments; (2) PhoneCo is now a better bet — avoid competing with Apple's brand in the consumer segment and own a niche with the business segment; (3) Neither acquisition makes sense now — too much uncertainty from a transformative new entrant, better to wait for the market to stabilize.

recommendation: SmartCo produces a phone that strongly appeals to consumers — the attributes consumers value most (Style, Price, Apps) are exactly where SmartCo outperforms PhoneCo by a wide margin.

The consumer segment will be roughly one-third of the total smartphone market in five years ($45b), but with only 15% smartphone penetration it still has enormous room for further growth — far more than the business segment (75% penetration) or prosumer segment.
SmartCo also has better unit economics: contribution margin of $100/unit vs. $100/unit for PhoneCo, but with a lower price point that should support higher volume in the mass-consumer market.
risks: Risk 1 — Competitive entry: A new player could enter the market specifically targeting consumers, eroding SmartCo's advantage.
Risk 2 — PhoneCo pivots: PhoneCo may recognize the consumer growth opportunity and reposition to compete in that segment.
Risk 3 — Shifting consumer preferences: Consumer attribute priorities may change as the market matures, potentially undermining SmartCo's current positioning advantage.
next_steps: Conduct deeper due diligence on SmartCo's technology, patents, and R&D pipeline to assess defensibility.
Model out unit economics at projected consumer market volumes to validate exit valuation.
Assess management team and operational capabilities for scaling to a mass-consumer market.
Monitor competitive landscape (including potential new entrants) before finalizing deal terms.
